sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is widely recognized as the strongest genetic risk factor for late‐onset Alzheimer's disease. Therapeutic strategies to reduce apoE4 expression in APOE ε4 carriers hold promise to mitigate neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative processes driving disease progression.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: Focused ultrasound (FUS) was employed to transiently open the blood–brain barrier (BBB) for efficient knockdown of humanized APOE ε4 in the mouse brain via gene editing. The all‐in‐one clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–based adeno‐associated virus (AAV) vectors were administered intravenously at a dose of 1.5×1012 vg per mouse to determine the gene‐editing efficacy within the hippocampus.

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: FUS‐enhanced delivery of AAV resulted in a 12.6% knockdown of APOE ε4 gene expression in the targeted hippocampus, accompanied by an over 20% decrease in apoE4 protein levels and significant reductions in astrocyte and microglia levels.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Our findings demonstrate a noninvasive, targeted approach for APOE ε4 knockdown, highlighting FUS‐mediated brain‐directed interventions as a promising therapeutic strategy for Alzheimer's disease.

list-item.p: Focused ultrasound (FUS) enables noninvasive, transient blood–brain barrier (BBB) opening for enhanced adeno‐associated virus (AAV) delivery.
FUS‐mediated gene editing achieves a 12.6% knockdown in APOE ε4 expression within the hippocampus of mouse brain.
APOE ε4 knockdown significantly reduces apoE4 protein levels and astrocyte and microglia levels.
No detectable gross toxicity was observed following the FUS‐mediated gene editing.

sec.title: BACKGROUND
sec.p: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the accumulation of amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques and hyperphosphorylated tau (p‐tau) neurofibrillary tangles, accompanied by synapse and neuron loss, neuritic dystrophy, vascular alterations, and inflammatory responses. 1 , 2 The apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele is the strongest genetic risk factor for late‐onset AD (LOAD). 3 Individuals carrying two copies of the ε4 allele have a 12‐fold higher risk of developing AD compared to those with the ε3 variant, and APOE ε4 is implicated in 55%–75% of AD dementia cases. 4 , 5 , 6 In AD pathogenesis, APOE ε4 promotes Aβ aggregation, enhances tau phosphorylation, disrupts lipid transport, and leads to cholesterol accumulation, collectively creating a neurotoxic environment that drives neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. 7 , 8 , 9 Consequently, reducing apoE4 expression in APOE ε4 carriers represents a promising therapeutic approach, as emphasized by the APOE4 National Institute on Aging/Alzheimer Disease Sequencing Project Consortium Working Group. 10

Current research is focused on brain‐specific approaches to reduce apoE4 levels using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), small‐interfering RNA (siRNA), and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). 11 , 12 , 13 However, these approaches often require repeated administrations. By contrast, genome editing via clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–CRISPR‐associated protein 9 (Cas9) offers the potential for precise, one‐time, and permanent therapeutic effects. 14 , 15 , 16 Despite this promise, efficient and targeted delivery of gene‐editing components to the brain remains a major challenge.

The blood–brain barrier (BBB) persists as the primary obstacle for brain‐directed therapeutics. This semi‐permeable barrier, characterized by tight junctions and efflux pumps, restricts the entry of most small‐molecule drugs and almost all macromolecular therapeutics, thereby constraining effective treatment options for central nervous system (CNS) disorders. 17 Focused ultrasound (FUS), in combination with intravenously administered microbubbles (MBs), provides a noninvasive, safe, and targeted technique to facilitate transient BBB opening (BBBO), bypassing these transport restrictions and enhancing the targeted delivery of therapeutic agents to the brain. 18 , 19 FUS traditionally employs a curved transducer, lens, or phased array to converge acoustic waves at a defined target, creating a localized high‐energy focal zone for amplified mechanical or thermal bioeffects. 18 , 19 MBs, typically composed of phospholipids, surfactants, or human serum albumin shells encapsulating an inert gas (usually perfluorocarbon), oscillate in response to ultrasound exposure within the brain vasculature, exerting mechanical forces on vessel walls to induce localized and reversible BBB permeabilization. 20 Over the past decades, FUS‐mediated BBBO has successfully facilitated the brain delivery of a variety of therapeutic, including small‐molecule drugs, 21 antibodies, 22 adeno‐associated viruses (AAVs), 23 , 24 , 25 and nanoparticles. 26 Preclinical studies in rodent and non‐human primate (NHP) models, both healthy and diseased, have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of FUS‐mediated BBBO. 25 , 27 Moreover, clinical trials are underway to evaluate FUS‐mediated BBBO for the treatment of primary and metastatic brain tumors (e.g., glioblastoma) and neurodegenerative diseases such as AD, Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). 19 , 21 , 22 , 28

list-item.p: Systematic review: The authors conducted a comprehensive literature review using traditional sources (e.g., PubMed), meeting abstracts, and presentations. Given that apolipoprotein E (APOE ε4) is the strongest genetic risk factor for late‐onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), lowering apoE4 levels has been widely explored as a therapeutic strategy. Various approaches to achieving this goal have been investigated, and the relevant studies are appropriately cited.

Interpretation: This study used focused ultrasound (FUS) to transiently open the blood–brain barrier (BBB) for enhanced adeno‐associated virus (AAV) delivery in the brain, enabling targeted knockdown of humanized APOE ε4, reduced expression of apoE4, and decreased astrocyte and microglia levels. This study represents the first noninvasive, systemic delivery of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)–based gene editing elements for APOE ε4 knockdown in a humanized mouse brain.

Future directions: This work highlights the potential of FUS‐mediated BBB opening as a noninvasive, precise, targeted platform to improve systemic delivery of gene‐editing tools in the brain. Future research could aim to engineer CRISPR‐based AAV systems, optimize FUS parameters for delivery of nonviral gene‐editing elements, expand studies to advanced transgenic AD mouse models and non‐human primates, and evaluate long‐term impacts on broader Alzheimer's disease pathology.

sec.p: In this study, we used FUS to induce transient BBBO, thereby enhancing the systemic delivery of AAV vectors carrying all‐in‐one CRISPR‐Cas9 and single‐guide RNA (sgRNA) construct designed specifically to target the humanized APOE ε4 gene in the mouse brain. Our results demonstrated that FUS‐mediated AAV administration in a single dose achieved significant APOE ε4 gene editing with minimal off‐target effects, reduced apoE4 protein levels, and decreased astrocyte and microglia levels. This noninvasive and targeted FUS‐based approach could be a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and other neurodegenerative disorders, which underscores the versatility of FUS‐based delivery technologies in facilitating precise and effective BBB penetration for CNS therapeutic interventions.

sec.title: Plasmid design
sec.p: The sgRNAs were designed with the protospacer‐adjacent motif (PAM) sequence (5′‐NNGRR‐3′) for Cas9 derived from Staphylococcus aureus (SaCas9). The sgRNAs target sites for CRISPR‐SaCas9‐based APOE ε4 knockdown were selected using CRISPick (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public) and CHOPCHOP (https://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/). The oligonucleotides were purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT). To design sgRNAs specifically targeting the APOE ε4 sequence encoding the apoE4 protein with arginine (Arg) at position 112, all potential sequences encompassing the “CGC” motif and PAM of 5′‐NNGRR‐3′ were evaluated. The sgRNAs were cloned into pX601‐mCherry plasmid (Addgene plasmid #84039) at the BsaI site, following a previously published protocol. 29 The plasmids were transformed into 5‐alpha competent Escherichia coli (New England Biolabs) and purified by using NucleoBond Xtra Midi Plus EF (Machrey‐Nagel), according to the manufacturer's instructions. The cloned vectors were verified via sequencing by Genewiz (Azenta Life Sciences).

The pX601‐AAV‐CMV::NLS‐SaCas9‐NLS‐3xHA‐bGHpA;U6::BsaI‐sgRNA (Addgene plasmid #61591) was used as the backbone for sgRNA1, sgRNA2, sgRNA3, and sgRNA4. The cytomegalovirus (CMV) promoter was replaced with the human synapsin (hSyn) promoter to validate in vivo gene editing. To accommodate AAV packaging constraints, the all‐in‐one plasmid lacked the mCherry reporter.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: Human apoE4‐overexpressing immortalized astrocyte cell line was used for in vitro gene editing validation. The cell line was derived from primary astrocyte cultures of human APOE4 knock‐in mice. 30 The cells were maintained in the medium composed of Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium/Nutrient Mixture F‐12 (DMEM/F‐12, Gibco), supplemented with Glutamax (Gibco), 10% fetal bovine serum (R&D systems), and 100 U/mL of penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco), in a humidified incubator at 37°C containing 5% CO2.

sec.title: Plasmid transfection and fluorescence‐activated cell sorting (FACS)
sec.p: Astrocytes were seeded into six‐well plates at a density of 300,000 cells/well. After 24 h, cells were transfected with 3 µg of plasmid using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen) per the manufacturer's protocol. Forty‐eight hours post‐transfection, transfected cells were harvested, and live mCherry‐positive cells were sorted using a SONY MA900 cell sorter.

sec.title: T7 endonuclease I (T7E1) assay
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from sorted astrocytes using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution (Epicentre) and amplified using Terra PCR Direct Polymerase Mix (Clontech) with the following cycling parameters: 98°C for 10 s, 68°C for 1 min, repeated for 35 cycles. DNA from astrocytes transfected with the hSyn‐promoter plasmid lacking mCherry was directly extracted without FACS. T7E1 mismatch cleavage assay was performed using Alt‐R Genome Editing Detection Kit (IDT) according to the manufacturer's instructions. sec.title: Sequencing
sec.p: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) products were purified by GeneJET Gel Extraction and DNA Cleanup Micro Kit (Thermo Scientific), and the concentration of the purified products was quantified using Quant‐iT PicoGreen dsDNA Assay Kits (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Sanger sequencing and next‐generation sequencing were conducted by Genewiz (Azenta Life Sciences). Indel mutations were analyzed using TIDE (http://shinyapps.datacurators.nl/tide/), 31 and deep sequencing data were processed with CRISPResso2 (http://crispresso2.pinellolab.org/submission). 32

sec.title: Reverse transcription‐quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT‐qPCR)
sec.p: RNA was extracted from sorted astrocytes using Quick DNA/RNA Miniprep Plus Kit (Zymo) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The concentration of the extracted RNA was measured using Quant‐iT RNA Assay Kits and Quant‐iT RNA HS Reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer's protocol. The extracted RNA was converted to complementary DNA (cDNA) using iScript cDNA Synthesis Kit (Bio‐Rad) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RT‐qPCR was conducted on QuantStudio 3 Real‐Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) using SsoAdvanced SYBR Green Supermix Kit (Bio‐Rad). Because the four sgRNAs target distinct exons of APOE ε4, four different primer pairs were designed to amplify the corresponding region surrounding the on‐target sites of each sgRNA. APOE4 messenger RNA (mRNA) expression levels were normalized to the expression levels of the housekeeping gene 18s ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

sec.title: Enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
sec.p: Protein was extracted from sorted astrocytes using Quick DNA/RNA Miniprep Plus Kit (Zymo) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The concentration of the extracted protein was measured by Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kits (Thermo Scientific) following the manufacturer's instructions. ApoE4 protein expression levels were quantified using the Human Apolipoprotein E ELISA Kit (Abcam, ab108813) according to the manufacturer's instructions, and normalized to the housekeeping GAPDH protein expression levels, which were measured using Mouse glyceraldehyde‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) ELISA Kit (RayBiotech) following the manufacturer's protocol.

sec.title: Mitochondrial membrane potential analysis
sec.p: The sorted astrocytes were seeded into 48‐well plates at a density of 30,000 cells/well. After 24 h, mitochondrial membrane potential was measured by tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE). The positive control carbonyl cyanide‐p‐trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone (FCCP) was applied to the control astrocytes without gene editing at the concentration of 5 µM for 10 min. The cells were incubated with 1 µM TMRE for 15 min, followed by washing once with 100 µL of phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS), and then viewed by microscope.

sec.title: Mice
sec.p: All animal studies were performed in compliance with the protocols AC‐AABU2665, AC‐AABG4559, and AC‐AABX4654, which were approved by the Columbia University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). We used transgenic APOE4KI (JAX Stock No. 027894) mice, commercially available from Jackson Laboratories, which carry humanized APOE ε4 homozygous genes (B6(SJL)‐ApoEtm1.1(APOE*4)Adiuj/J). 33 All animals were housed with littermates and maintained on a 12‐h light/dark cycle with ad libitum access to chow and water.

sec.title: FUS‐mediated BBBO for enhanced AAV delivery
FUS system
sec.p: The FUS transducer, a P4‐1 (ATL, Philips) phased array (2.5 MHz center frequency, 1.5‐3.5 MHz ‐6 dB bandwidth, 96 elements), was controlled by a three‐dimensional (3D) positioning system (VXM, Velmex Inc., Bloomfield, New York, USA) and operated using a research ultrasound system (Vantage 256 system, Verasonics Inc., Kirkland, Washington, USA). A custom MATLAB script was used to generate rapid bursts of short pulses with a transmit frequency of 1.5 MHz and pulse length of ≈3 half cycles, as described previously. 24 , 34 The focal depth of focused transmits was 35 mm from the face of the transducer. The estimated free‐field peak negative pressure transmitted was 1.5 MPa. The total treatment time was 2 min, during which 60 bursts were delivered, with burst repetition frequency (BRF) of 0.5 Hz. Each burst contained 100 focused pulses transmitted at a pulse repetition frequency (PRF) of 1000 Hz. 24

sec.title: Microbubbles (MBs)
sec.p: Polydisperse MBs were formulated in‐house following previously published protocols. 35 A lipid mixture of 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphocholine (DSPC, Avanti Polar Lipids) and 1,2‐distearoyl‐sn‐glycero‐3‐phosphoethanolamine‐N‐[methoxy(polyethylene glycol)‐2000] (DSPC‐mPEG2000, Avanti Polar Lipids) at a molar ratio of 9:1 was dissolved in a solution containing PBS, glycerol (10% volume) and propylene glycol (10% volume) at a concentration of 2 mg/mL. The lipids were fully dissolved using a sonication bath maintained above 60°C for 1–2 h. Then, the solution was aliquoted into 5 mL vials with rubber stoppers and flip caps for storage at 4°C until use. Before the FUS procedure, the MBs were activated by vacuuming out air and replacing it with perfluorobutane gas (C4F10) a total of five times. Subsequently, they were mechanically agitated by using a VialMix shaker (Lantheus Medical Imaging) for 45 s. The size distribution and concentration of the activated MBs were evaluated by particle counter (Multisizer 4e Coulter Counter, Beckman Coulter).

sec.title: BBBO procedure and intravenous (i.v.) injection of AAVs
sec.p: The adult mouse (8 weeks old) was first anesthetized with 3%–4% isoflurane. A surgical plane of anesthesia was confirmed using the toe pinch withdrawal reflex test. The mouse was then placed on a heating pad and the head was fixed in a stereotactic frame (David Kopf Instruments) under continuous anesthesia delivered through a nose cone with 1%–2% isoflurane during the treatment. The scalp was shaved and treated with depilatory cream to ensure complete hair removal. Degassed ultrasound gel, prepared by centrifugation at 2000 rpm for 20 min, was then applied over the scalp to facilitate acoustic coupling. Subsequently, a water bath containing degassed deionized water was placed above the mouse's head.

To target the desired region in the brain, the intersection of the lambdoid and sagittal sutures on the mouse skull was first identified, which was visible through the depilated scalp. A metal crosshair was then positioned at lambda to align the intersecting lines along the lateral and elevational dimensions of the transducer. The transducer was subsequently submerged in the water bath and B‐mode imaging at 2.5 MHz was obtained to position the transducer over the target focal area marked by a red circle. The FUS transducer was positioned over the left hemisphere, 3 mm anterior and 2 mm lateral relative to the cranial landmark lambda, whereas the right hemisphere was designated as the untreated control. After targeting was confirmed, the metal crosshair was removed.

Immediately before the FUS procedures, an appropriate amount of in‐house‐made polydisperse MBs was mixed with 100 µL of sterile saline solution to reach a final MBs concentration of 8×108 MB/mL. The left hemisphere was first sonicated for 10 s to obtain a baseline signal. Sonication was initiated, followed by the i.v. administration of MBs into the lateral tail vein of the mouse using a 27G butterfly needle scalp vein set. After MBs administration, the AAV solution was administered intravenously at a dose of 1.5×1012 vector genomes (vg)/mouse. The AAV9 was produced and titered by the Zuckerman Institute Virology Core. In the control group, only the MBs solution was administered intravenously without any AAV injection. The total sonication duration after MBs injection was 2 min. Upon completion of the procedure, the needle was removed from the tail, and the mouse was released from the stereotactic frame and allowed to recover from anesthesia. Five mice were assigned to each group, including two males and three females, resulting in a total of five groups: four groups treated with AAV, each containing a different sgRNA; and one control group that underwent FUS only without AAV injection.

sec.title: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and BBBO volume calculation
sec.p: Following the FUS procedure, 0.2 mL of gadodiamide (Gd)–based contrast agent (Omniscan, GE Healthcare) was administered intraperitoneally (i.p.) to the mouse to detect BBBO on MRI. The mouse was anesthetized and positioned in a 30 mm diameter birdcage coil to confirm BBBO by using a 9.4T MRI system (Bruker Medical). Contrast‐enhanced T1‐weighted 2D fast low angle shot (FLASH) MRI images were acquired in both the axial and coronal planes (repetition time/echo time [TR/TE]: 230/3.3 ms; flip angle: 70°; average: 6; field of view: 25.6×25.6 mm2; resolution: 100×100×400 µm3). The BBBO volume was calculated from MRI images using a custom MATLAB script (n = 5).

In addition, T2‐RARE sequence was performed prior to contrast injection in both the axial and coronal planes (TR/TE: 2500/30 ms; average: 6; field of view: 25.6×25.6 mm2; resolution: 100×100×400 µm3) to assess for potential hemorrhage or edema.

sec.title: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining
sec.p: At Days 0 and 2 following FUS treatment, mice were anesthetized and transcardially perfused with 20 mL of cold 1× PBS, followed by 20 mL of cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS. Brains were collected, post‐fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin, and coronally sectioned into 5 µm slices. H&E staining and imaging were performed by the Columbia HICCC Molecular Pathology Core.

sec.title: Sequencing
sec.p: Three weeks post‐treatment, the FUS‐treated mice were anesthetized and transcardially perfused with 20 mL of cold 1× PBS, followed by 20 mL of cold 4% PFA in PBS. Genomic DNA was separately extracted from the left and right hippocampus using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution (Epicentre). As described previously, the extracted DNA was then amplified, purified, and prepared for deep sequencing by Plasmidsaurus. The resulting deep sequencing data were analyzed using CRISPResso2. 32 Five mice were tested each group.

sec.title: RT‐qPCR
sec.p: RNA from the left and right hippocampus was separately extracted using Quick DNA/RNA Miniprep Plus Kit (Zymo) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The concentration of the extracted RNA was measured using Quant‐iT RNA Assay Kits and Quant‐iT RNA HS Reagent (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer's protocol. The extracted RNA was converted to cDNA using iScript cDNA Synthesis Kit (Bio‐Rad) according to the manufacturer's instructions. RT‐qPCR was conducted on QuantStudio 3 Real‐Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) using SsoAdvanced SYBR Green Supermix Kit (Bio‐Rad). Because the four sgRNAs target distinct exons of APOE ε4, four different primer pairs were designed to amplify the corresponding region surrounding the on‐target sites of each sgRNA. APOE4 mRNA expression levels were normalized to the expression levels of the housekeeping gene 18s rRNA. For each mouse, the relative ratio of normalized RNA expression levels in the left hippocampus (AAV‐injected and FUS‐treated) to the right hippocampus (AAV‐injected only, without FUS) was calculated. As for the control group, the left hippocampus treated with FUS but without AAV injection was compared to the untreated right hippocampus. Five mice were tested for each group.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and confocal imaging
sec.p: The collected brains were post‐fixed in 4% PFA, embedded in paraffin, and coronally sectioned into 5 µm slides. The sections were deparaffinized with xylene, rehydrated through a graded ethanol series, and subjected to antigen retrieval using eBioscience IHC Antigen Retrieval Solution (Invitrogen). The sections were then rinsed in TBS‐Tween 20 (Thermo Scientific) and blocked with 10% goat serum in TBS‐Tween 20 for 1 h at room temperature. The sections were incubated overnight at 4°C in the blocking buffer containing primary antibodies. After three 10‐min washes in TBS‐Tween 20, the sections were incubated in blocking buffer containing secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. The sections were subsequently washed three times for 10 min each in TBS‐Tween 20 and mounted with ProLong Gold Antifade Mountant with DNA Stain DAPI (Invitrogen). The following primary antibodies were used: rabbit anti‐ApoE (1:500, Abcam, ab52607), chicken anti‐GFAP (1:500, Abcam, ab4674), rabbit anti‐S100β (1:500, Abcam, ab52642), rabbit anti‐Iba1 (1:500, Wako, 019‐19741), chicken anti‐CD68 (1:500, Abcam, ab318303), and mouse anti‐BASE‐tag (clone 7C7, recognize AAV9 capsid protein VP1, 1:150, Millipore Sigma, MAB131884). The following secondary antibodies were used: Alexa Fluor 488 goat anti‐rabbit (1:500, Abcam, ab150077), Alexa Fluor 594 goat anti‐chicken (1:500, Abcam, ab150172), and Alexa Fluor 647 goat anti‐mouse (1:500, Invitrogen, A21235).

Imaging was performed using Nikon Ti2 inverted microscope with AXR resonant spectral scanning confocal unit under 10× and 60× magnification. The co‐localization of apoE4 and GFAP, as well as the number and coverage area of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ionized calcium‐binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1), were quantified using Imaris 10.2 (Oxford Instruments) with the AI‐based Filament Tracer for linear branching networks. The coverage area of S100 calcium‐binding protein β (S100β) and CD68 was quantified by ImageJ. The cornu ammonis (CA) and dentate gyrus (DG) regions of hippocampus were quantified separately, and the number or coverage area of each marker was measured per mm2. For each mouse, the relative ratio of each protein marker in the left hippocampus (AAV‐injected and FUS‐treated) to the right hippocampus (AAV‐injected only, without FUS) was calculated. For the control group, the left hippocampus treated with FUS but without AAV injection was compared to the untreated right hippocampus. Five mice were tested each group.

sec.title: ELISA
sec.p: Protein from the left and right hippocampus was extracted separately using Quick DNA/RNA Miniprep Plus Kit (Zymo) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The concentration of the extracted protein was measured by Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kits (Thermo Scientific) following the manufacturer's instructions. ApoE4 protein expression levels were quantified using Human Apolipoprotein E ELISA Kit (Abcam, ab108813) according to the manufacturer's instructions, and normalized to the housekeeping GAPDH protein expression levels, which were measured using Mouse GAPDH ELISA Kit (RayBiotech) following the manufacturer's protocol. For each mouse, the relative ratio of normalized protein expression levels in the left hippocampus (AAV‐injected and FUS‐treated) to the right hippocampus (AAV‐injected only, without FUS) was calculated. In the control group, the left hippocampus treated with FUS but without AAV injection was compared to the untreated right hippocampus. Five mice were tested each group.

sec.title: RNA in situ hybridization (ISH)
sec.p: ISH was performed on paraffin‐embedded brain sections of four groups: FUS‐treated, non‐treated, FUS+AAV‐sgRNA2‐treated, and AAV‐sgRNA2‐treated. Slides were deparaffinized and pretreated following the manufacturer's instructions, using RNAscope Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v2 (Advanced Cell Diagnostics, 323100). Probes used included Mm‐Gfap (313211), saCas9 (501621‐C2), and Hs‐APOE (433091‐C3), in combination with TSA Vivid Fluorophore 520 (PN 323271), TSA Vivid Fluorophore 570 (PN 323272), and TSA Vivid Fluorophore 650 (PN 323273), following the manufacturer's instructions. Imaging was performed using Nikon Ti2 inverted microscope with AXR resonant spectral scanning confocal unit under 20× and 60× magnification. Cells were classified as positive for a gene if they contained ≥5 RNA spots as determined by manual quantification. Five mice were tested each group.

sec.title: Off‐target test
sec.p: Cas‐OFFinder (http://www.rgenome.net/cas‐offinder/) was used to predict potential off‐target sites of sgRNA2 in both mouse and human genomes. 36 For the mouse genome, DNA was extracted from the hippocampus treated with FUS and AAVs encoding sgRNA2, as well as from the control hippocampus without any treatment. For the human genome, DNA was extracted from HEK 293T cells treated with the all‐in‐one plasmid containing hSyn promoter and sgRNA2, and from untreated cells. The extracted DNA was amplified using Platinum SuperFi II PCR Master Mixes (Invitrogen) with the following cycling parameters: 98°C for 10 s, 60°C for 10 s, and 72°C for 15s, repeated for 35 cycles. The amplified products were then subjected to the T7E1 assay and Sanger sequencing as described previously.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted using Prism 9.0 (GraphPad). Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). The significance of differences was determined using unpaired two‐tailed Student's t‐tests. Intergroup differences were considered statistically significant at *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, and ****p < 0.0001.

sec.title: In vitro sgRNA screening for APOE ε4 knockdown
sec.p: To efficiently disrupt the human APOE ε4 gene, we designed four sgRNAs targeting distinct exons (Figure 1A). Specifically, sgRNA1 and sgRNA2 targeted exon 3, whereas sgRNA3 and sgRNA4 targeted exon 4. The sequences of these sgRNAs are listed in Table S1. Each sgRNA was individually cloned into a plasmid containing SaCas9 and mCherry marker, allowing FACS‐based selection post‐transfection. Given that apoE is expressed predominantly in astrocytes, we assessed the knockdown efficiency of each sgRNA using astrocytes from humanized APOE4KI mice. 5 , 30 To evaluate editing efficiency, three PCR fragments were amplified to cover the target site of each sgRNA (Figure 1B, gray segments). The fragment PCR1 (393 bp) encompassed exon 3, including the on‐target sites of sgRNA1 and sgRNA2, with expected SaCas9‐induced cleavage products of 135 + 258 bp and 299 + 94 bp, respectively. The fragment PCR2 (350 bp) spanned the sgRNA3 target site in the anterior exon 4, with predicted cleavage of 111 + 239 bp, whereas the fragment PCR3 (567 bp) covered the sgRNA4 target site in the posterior exon 4, with anticipated cleavage of 221 + 346 bp. T7E1 assay confirmed CRISPR‐induced cleavage at all target sites (Figures 1B, S1), aligning with the predicted cleavage products. Analysis of T7E1‐digested versus undigested bands (Figure 1B,C) revealed mutation frequencies of 39.9% (sgRNA1), 52% (sgRNA2), 37.2% (sgRNA3), and 26.6% (sgRNA4), with sgRNA2 showing the highest APOE ε4 editing efficiency.

sec.p: Sanger sequencing also validated successful cleavage for each sgRNA at the intended target site (Figure S2a‐d). Unlike the homogeneous sequences in untreated astrocytes, sgRNA‐transfected astrocytes exhibited heterogeneous sequences beginning at the cleavage site (the red arrowhead). CRISPR‐Cas9 induced double‐strand breaks between nucleotides 17 and 18 of the sgRNA sequence, and subsequent NHEJ repair introduced sequence diversification beyond the cleavage site, potentially leading to frameshift mutations and loss‐of‐function alleles. 37 TIDE analysis quantified the insertion‐deletion mutations (InDels) through sequence decomposition (Figure S2e‐h), again highlighting sgRNA2 as the most effective candidate with an editing efficacy of 57.2%. Deep sequencing further provided a comprehensive breakdown of mutation types, including insertions, deletions, and substitutions (Figures 1D,E, S3). Overall genome‐editing efficacies for sgRNA1, sgRNA2, sgRNA3, and sgRNA4 were 50.6%, 73.6%, 45.4%, and 44%, respectively. Notably, deep sequencing data indicated higher editing efficiencies than the T7E1 assay, likely due to the greater sensitivity and single‐base resolution of next‐generation sequencing compared to the T7E1 assay, which relies on heteroduplex formation and has a limited dynamic range. 38 Collectively, these data indicate that sgRNA2 demonstrates superior APOE ε4 knockdown capability. Moreover, apoE4 protein expression in astrocytes following APOE ε4 knockdown for sgRNA1, sgRNA2, sgRNA3, and sgRNA4 was reduced to 53.4%, 39.4%, 63%, and 71.7%, respectively (Figure 1F). Correspondingly, APOE4 mRNA expression levels were reduced to 63.4%, 50.3%, 68.8%, and 75.1%, respectively (Figure 1G). In addition, mitochondrial membrane potential analysis indicated that the apoE4 fragments generated after gene editing did not induce significant mitochondrial toxicity (Figure S4).

Given that the only differences among apoE isoforms occur at positions 112 and 158, we designed allele‐specific sgRNAs targeting the APOE ε4‐unique “CGC” codon encoding Arg112 (Figure S5a, Table S1). 12 However, T7E1 assay, Sanger sequencing, and TIDE analysis all showed negligible editing activity for these allele‐specific sgRNAs (Figure S5b‐d), suggesting that APOE ε4‐specific editing remains challenging with the SaCas9 system.

To enhance in vivo editing efficiency, we replaced the CMV promoter with the neuron‐specific hSyn promoter, 39 and removed the mCherry tag to accommodate the AAV package limitation of ≈4.7 kb. 37 In the absence of FACS‐based selection post‐transfection, T7E1 assay revealed APOE ε4 knockdown efficiencies of 23% (sgRNA1), 34.5% (sgRNA2), 26.8% (sgRNA3), and 12% (sgRNA4) (Figure S6a). sgRNA2 remained the most efficient, confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure S6b‐e) and TIDE analysis (Figure S6f‐i). The all‐in‐one CRISPR‐SaCas9 plasmids were subsequently packed into AAV9 vectors for in vivo gene editing, leveraging the superior CNS transduction capacity of AAV9 serotypes. 40 Moreover, AAV9 is one of the few AAV serotypes that has been approved clinically for therapeutic use, supported by extensive pre‐clinical, clinical, and post‐marketing safety data. 41

sec.title: FUS enhanced AAV delivery for APOE ε4 knockdown in mouse brain
sec.p: We used the P4‐1 transducer connected to the Vantage system for precise BBBO and simultaneous cavitation imaging (Figure 2A). 24 , 25 The underlying mechanism of FUS‐mediated BBBO relies on acoustic cavitation of MBs, influenced by multiple parameters such as frequency, pressure, pulse length, BRF, PRF, sonication duration, and concentration of MBs. 19 Here we use acoustic parameters that, according to our previous studies, have resulted in high AAV delivery efficacy while ensuring safety following BBB opening. 24 , 25 , 34 As illustrated in Figure 2B, intravenously administered MBs oscillate within the FUS focus, opening endothelial tight junctions and transiently enhancing BBB permeability, thereby facilitating targeted AAV delivery to the hippocampus. 18 , 19 With the FUS parameters used herein, cavitation‐induced stress remains tolerable for the vasculature, and BBB integrity rapidly recovers without hemorrhagic or ischemic complications. 24 , 34

sec.p: The experimental timeline is outlined in Figure 2C. We used cross‐sectional B‐mode imaging to accurately align the P4‐1 transducer over the left hemisphere of the mouse before FUS treatment (Figure 2D). With the sonication parameters shown in Figure 2E, cavitation imaging after MBs injection markedly increased (Figure 2F, right) relative to baseline (Figure 2F, left), indicating acoustic cavitation and localized BBB permeability changes. Total sonication lasted for 2 min, during which AAV9 vectors were administered at a dose of 1.5×1012 vg per mouse. To confirm successful BBBO, contrast‐enhanced T1‐weighted MRI was performed 30 min post‐FUS, showing localized enhancement of Gd‐based contrast agents in the sonicated hemisphere (Figure 2G). The average volume of FUS‐induced BBBO was 82.67 ± 3.33 mm3 (Figure S7a). Moreover, T2‐weighted MRI confirmed the safety of the procedure, showing no apparent edema or hemorrhage (Figure S7b). AAV9 distribution was assessed 12 h post‐sonication via IHC using an anti‐BASE tag antibody against the AAV9 capsid protein VP1. IHC image revealed increased AAV localization in the FUS‐targeted left hippocampus (Figure 2H), indicating improved AAV delivery after sonication. To evaluate reversibility of BBBO, a Gd‐based contrast agent was re‐administered 48 h post‐treatment, followed by T1‐weighted MRI. No contrast enhancement was observed in the previously sonicated regions (Figure 2I), confirming complete restoration of BBB integrity within 48 h. In addition, H&E staining revealed minimal red blood cell extravasation at Day 0 following FUS, which fully subsided by Day 2 (Figure S7c), further confirming the safety of FUS‐induced BBBO. These results demonstrate that our optimized FUS parameters enable efficient, targeted, and reversible BBBO, significantly enhanced AAV delivery across the BBB.

We observed significant APOE ε4 editing in the left hippocampus of mice receiving intravenously administered AAVs alongside FUS treatment (Figures 3A, S8, S9a), showing a more than five‐fold increase compared to the right hippocampus without FUS treatment across all sgRNAs. Consistent with in vitro results, sgRNA2 demonstrated the highest APOE ε4 knockdown efficiency, achieving 12.6% editing in the FUS‐treated left hippocampus, compared to only 2.2% in the right hippocampus without FUS treatment. The other sgRNAs showed less than 8% editing events with the assistance of FUS, indicating the critical role of sgRNA design for efficient genome editing. To evaluate the impact on gene editing, we analyzed APOE4 mRNA expression by calculating the relative left hippocampus (AAV‐injected and FUS‐treated) to the right hippocampus (AAV‐injected only, without FUS) ratio. In the sgRNA2‐treated group, APOE4 mRNA expression decreased significantly to 0.79 (Figures 3B, S9b), corresponding to a 21% reduction caused by FUS‐enhanced gene editing. In the control groups, which received FUS in the left hippocampus and no treatment in the right, the ratio remained near 1.0, confirming that FUS alone does not influence mRNA expression.

sec.p: We subsequently investigated apoE4 protein expression following APOE ε4 knockdown. IHC staining revealed significantly reduced apoE4‐positive signals in the left hippocampus of FUS‐mediated AAV delivery groups, whereas no significant reduction was observed in the FUS‐only or AAV‐only groups compared to the untreated group (Figure 3C). This suggests that FUS alone does not reduce apoE4 protein levels. Moreover, systemic AAV administration without FUS resulted in limited BBB penetration, yielding only 1%–2% gene editing (Figure 3A), which was insufficient to significantly affect apoE4 expression. Given that apoE is expressed predominantly by astrocytes under physiological conditions, constituting ≈75%–80% of total brain apoE, 5 we further quantified apoE4‐positive astrocytes by staining for GFAP. Consistent with genome editing results, the combination of FUS and AAV significantly reduced the number of apoE4‐positive GFAP‐stained astrocytes (Figure 3D,E). Notably, GFAP‐stained cell counts remained constant across groups (Figure 4), demonstrating that reductions in the apoE4‐positive GFAP ratio accurately reflected apoE4 protein reduction rather than astrocyte loss. Similarly, the left‐to‐right hippocampus apoE4‐positive GFAP ratio was calculated (Figures 3F,G, S9c,d), with the sgRNA2 group showing ratios of 0.74 in the CA region and 0.8 in the DG regions, indicating more than 20% decrease in apoE4 expression due to FUS‐mediated genome editing. In addition, the normalized apoE4 expression in the overall hippocampus was quantified using ELISA (Figures 3H, S9e), and the relative ratio of left to right hippocampus was calculated. Consistent with IHC results, the sgRNA2‐treated group exhibited a significantly reduced ratio of 0.77, corresponding to a 23% decrease in apoE4 protein expression in the hippocampus area due to FUS‐assisted gene knockdown. In addition, RNAscope‐based ISH was used to verify the reduction of APOE4 mRNA, revealing ≈13.6% decrease in GFAP+ astrocytes (Figure S10a‐c). Furthermore, ISH showed co‐expression of SaCas9 and GFAP mRNA in ≈12.9% of cells in the FUS + AAV‐treated group, compared to ≈2.6% in the AAV‐only treated group, confirming the enhanced gene editing efficiency in astrocytes mediated by FUS (Figure S10a,b,d). These results underscore the effectiveness of FUS‐mediated BBBO for enhanced AAV delivery and highlight the importance of optimized sgRNAs for robust brain gene editing. When APOE ε4 editing exceeded 10%, both apoE4 protein and APOE4 mRNA levels in the hippocampus decreased by ≈20%, presenting a promising therapeutic strategy to treat LOAD.

sec.p: Given the superior APOE ε4 editing efficiency of sgRNA2, we examined potential off‐target effects at the top five computationally predicted sites in both HEK 293T cells (representing the human genome) and mouse brain tissue (Figure S11a,d). T7E1 analysis showed no obvious cleavage bands in sgRNA2‐treated groups (Figure S11b,e), whereas Sanger sequencing revealed no differences between control samples and the sgRNA2‐treated samples (Figure S11c,f), indicating that off‐target events in both human and mouse genomes were rare. These results support the safety and therapeutic potential of sgRNA2 for further preclinical development.

sec.title: Decreased astrocyte levels following APOE ε4 knockdown
sec.p: APOE ε4 is known to promote astrocyte and microglia expression levels. 5 We observed a significantly decreased astrocyte levels following APOE ε4 knockdown (Figure 4A,B,F). To quantify the extent of astrocyte reduction, we assessed the expression of GFAP and S100β, 42 calculating the ratio between the left (FUS‐treated) and right (without FUS treatment) hippocampus. Following FUS‐mediated AAV delivery, GFAP cell counts remained unchanged across the CA and DG regions in all sgRNA‐treated groups (Figures 4C,G, S12a,d). In contrast, the GFAP‐positive and S100β‐positive areas were reduced, especially in the sgRNA2‐treated group with the highest APOE ε4 knockdown efficiency. In the sgRNA2‐treated group, the GFAP‐positive area decreased to 0.74 in the CA region and 0.78 in the DG region of the left hippocampus, compared to the right hippocampus without FUS treatment (Figures 4D,H, S12b,e). Similarly, the S100β coverage area was markedly reduced in the left hippocampus of sgRNA2‐treated mice, with values of 0.63 in the CA region and 0.7 in the DG region (Figures 4E,I, S12c,f). It is important to note that the FUS‐only control group showed no observable changes in GFAP cell counts, GFAP‐positive area, or S100β‐positive area between the left and right hippocampus, indicating that the reductions in astrocyte level were not attributable to FUS treatment alone. Collectively, these results suggest that APOE ε4 knockdown, accompanied by decreased apoE4 expression, led to reduced astrocyte levels.

sec.title: Decreased microglia levels following APOE ε4 knockdown
sec.p: Furthermore, we observed a marked decrease in microglia levels following APOE ε4 editing by staining Iba1 and CD68. Iba1 is a widely used microglia marker identifying both resting microglia in healthy brain tissue and activated microglia in response to injury, inflammation, or neurodegeneration. 43 CD68 is a macrophage marker expressed in functionally activated microglia, which is upregulated during inflammatory response, facilitating phagocytosis and clearance of cellular debris, pathogens, or damaged neurons. 43 FUS‐mediated AAV delivery decreased both Iba1‐positive and CD68‐positive microglia, particularly in the sgRNA2‐treated group (Figure 5A,B,F). The counts and coverage area of Iba1‐positive microglia in the CA region dropped to 0.94 and 0.89, respectively (Figures 5C,D, S13a,b), with more pronounced decreases in the DG region (0.85 and 0.83, respectively) (Figures 5G,H, S13d,e). Similarly, the CD68‐positive area was reduced significantly in the sgRNA2‐treated group, with values of 0.72 in the CA region and 0.66 in the DG region (Figures 5E,I, S13c,f). Notably, the FUS‐only control group displayed no observable changes in Iba1 number, Iba1‐positive area, or CD68‐positive area between the left and right hippocampus, confirming that these reductions were not caused by FUS treatment alone. Together, these results suggest that APOE ε4 knockdown, with consequent reductions in apoE4 expression, resulting in decreased microglial levels and mitigated neuroinflammation.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: In this study, we demonstrated that FUS‐induced BBBO significantly improved brain‐targeted gene editing efficacy following systemic administration of all‐in‐one CRISPR‐based AAVs. This approach achieved robust knockdown of humanized APOE ε4 allele in the transgenic mouse hippocampus, leading to a marked reduction in APOE4 mRNA and apoE4 protein expression and decreased astrocyte and microglia levels with minimal off‐target effects. These findings establish FUS‐mediated BBBO as a noninvasive, precise, and targeted approach for systemic delivery of gene‐editing elements to correct disease‐causing mutations in the brain, providing a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and other neurodegenerative disorders.

Because APOE ε4 is the primary genetic risk factor for LOAD, lowering its expression holds considerable therapeutic potential by alleviating Aβ and tau pathologies, mitigating neuroinflammation, preserving neuronal and synaptic function, and maintaining cerebrovascular integrity. 11 Recognizing its importance, the APOE4 National Institute on Aging/Alzheimer Disease Sequencing Project Consortium Working Group has prioritized therapeutic strategies targeting apoE4 reduction. 10 Our study achieved targeted APOE ε4 editing of 12.6%, leading to more than 20% reduction in hippocampal apoE4 expression. Previous studies suggest that a 50% reduction in CNS apoE4 is well tolerated in mice. 11 In addition, our CRISPR‐based approach enables permanent reductions in apoE4 expression with minimal off‐target effects, thus offering a potentially curative intervention that directly addresses the mutation at its source while minimizing the risks and side effects associated with repeated dosing required by other therapeutic methods. 44

One of the most significant challenges in brain‐directed gene editing lies in traversing the BBB, which severely restricts the CNS delivery of many therapeutic agents, particularly biologics. Although direct intracranial injection of AAVs has recently shown localized knockdown of mouse APOE in the brain, 45 this invasive procedure poses considerable risks, including intracranial hemorrhage, tissue damage, and infection. 46 Most importantly, local administration is inadequate to treat neurodegenerative diseases like AD, which affect multiple brain regions. 47 In contrast, FUS‐mediated BBBO addresses these limitations by facilitating noninvasive, wide‐spreading, and targeted delivery of therapeutic agents to the brain. 18 Its safety and efficacy have been validated extensively in numerous preclinical and clinical studies. 27 Notably, we have recently completed a study using a portable, neuronavigation‐guided, single‐element FUS system to achieve safe BBBO in AD patients (NCT04118764). 28 Moreover, safety concerns regarding FUS‐induced BBBO have been largely mitigated through optimized parameters such as frequency and pressure. 19 Our previous studies also showed that transient inflammatory responses observed post‐BBBO, including temporary activation of astrocytes and microglia, typically resolve within days. 25 , 48 , 49 , 50 Building upon the improved safety profiles, we were the first to report FUS‐mediated delivery of CRISPR‐based AAVs in mouse brain for efficient neuronal gene editing in Ai9 and TLR2 mouse models. 24

In this study, we expanded this FUS‐based approach to achieve knockdown of humanized APOE ε4 in the mouse hippocampal astrocytes for potential AD treatment. We employed the CRISPR‐SaCas9 system because its smaller size allows the packaging of SaCas9 and its sgRNA within a single AAV vector, which avoids the complexity and low efficacy of two‐vector SpCas9 strategies. 37 Through rational design and systematic screening of sgRNAs for SaCas9 to target humanized APOE ε4, we achieved a gene editing efficacy of 12.6% in the hippocampus, which is one of the earliest regions affected in AD for memory processing and storage. 51 The observed reduction in astrocyte and microglial levels in 3‐month‐old mice is consistent with previous findings, where astrocytic APOE ε4 knockdown in APPPS1/FE4/Cre+ mice at 4 weeks of age—prior to Aβ plaque formation—resulted in decreased astrocyte and microglia activation at 18 weeks of age, along with reduced Aβ plaque deposition and accumulation. 52 Additional studies have also been performed where APOE4 was removed in middle‐aged mice, with assessments conducted at later disease stages. 53 , 54 Unlike these studies, when APOE ε4‐induced astrogliosis and microgliosis were rather pronounced, our findings suggest that early APOE ε4 knockdown in young mice can reduce astrocytic and microglial levels at earlier stages as well. Indeed, diminished astrocytic apoE4 expression has been linked to decreased amyloid plaque accumulation, tau‐mediated neurodegeneration, synaptic loss, and neuroinflammation. 52 , 53

Early preventative treatment before the onset of pathology holds significant promise for effective AD therapy. Even at a young age, APOE4 mice exhibit early‐stage AD characteristics. For instance, 3‐month‐old APOE4 mice display metabolic alterations in astrocytes and microglia compared to APOE3 mice, albeit less severe than in aged mice. 55 Moreover, APOE4 mice have been reported to exhibit increased levels of Aβ42 and p‐tau in the hippocampus by 4 months of age. 56 Cognitive deficits, particularly impaired spatial learning and memory, have been observed as early as 3 months in APOE4 mice, as demonstrated with the Barnes maze. 57 Supporting this preventative treatment goal, APOE ASOs administered before Aβ deposition reduced Aβ deposition by ≈50% and significantly decreased Aβ‐associated neuritic dystrophy, whereas administration after Aβ deposition showed limited effects. 58 Although further validation is still required, our findings suggest that early APOE ε4 knockdown might be a promising treatment strategy before significant pathology develops, and that FUS‐mediated BBBO could aid in that process.

A key advantage of our FUS‐based approach is the significantly lower AAV dose (1.5×1012 vg per mouse, ≈6.0×1013 vg/kg) compared to previous systemic delivery studies. For example, a previous report that disrupted the mutated amyloid‐beta precursor protein (APP) in the mouse brain, which is the precursor to Aβ peptide to determine Aβ production levels, required 1×1013 vg per mouse of AAV‐PHP.eB via retro‐orbital injection. 59 In addition, our AAV9 dose falls within the clinically acceptable safety range of 1012–1014 vg/kg. 60 For reference, Zolgensma, an AAV9‐based therapy for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), is administered intravenously at a dose of 1.1×1014 vg/kg. 41 Our findings reiterate that FUS‐mediated BBBO significantly reduces the AAV dose required for systemic delivery, representing a crucial advantage for potential clinical translation.

Future investigations could improve the efficiency and specificity of this approach by engineering CRISPR‐based AAV components, such as selecting AAV serotypes with improved CNS penetration. 61 For example, AAV‐F, an AAV9 variant with a seven‐amino acid insertion in the VP1 region, achieved over 65‐fold higher transgene expression in cortical astrocytes than parental AAV9, 62 which can be an alternative approach to FUS or further reduce the required dose of AAVs to eliminate side effects through combination with FUS. Developing SaCas9 variants with alternative PAM compatibilities to broaden the range of target sites for allele‐specific APOE ε4 knockdown is another promising method. 63 Beyond gene knockdown, base editing offers an alternative strategy to correct APOE ε4 to APOE ε3 via precise C‐to‐T nucleotide conversions. 16 However, splitting large base editing constructs across two AAV vectors introduces technical challenges, including reduced editing efficacy, inconsistent editing outcomes, and immunogenicity risks. 64 , 65 Another promising direction is to employ nonviral vectors, such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), polymers, and inorganic nanoparticles, to overcome the packaging limitation of AAVs. 66 Unlike AAVs, nonviral vectors typically provide transient gene expression, reducing potential off‐target effects. 67 Moreover, their lower immunogenicity allows repeated dosing, which is not feasible for AAVs due to the generation of neutralizing antibodies. 68 Advances in the synthesis and functionalization of nanomaterials could also facilitate efficient tissue‐ or cell‐specific targeting. 69 Promising safety profiles of LNPs have been reported in both mice and NHPs to support robust gene editing, with initial clinical data also showing favorable tolerability. 70 Nevertheless, the synthesized nanomaterials are usually larger than the 25 nm AAVs, 71 , 72 requiring further optimization of FUS parameters to ensure effective brain‐wide delivery. Notably, repeated FUS treatments alone have been shown to reduce Aβ plaques and p‐tau levels, enhance neurogenesis, and improve cognitive function. 73 , 74 , 75 A recent clinical study combining FUS with aducanumab infusion has demonstrated Aβ reduction over multiple monthly treatment cycles in patients. 22 These findings suggest that integrating APOE ε4 knockdown with repeated FUS treatments may enhance therapeutic outcomes in AD.

This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of FUS‐mediated delivery of CRISPR‐based gene editing elements for targeted humanized APOE ε4 knockdown in the mouse hippocampus. Although our findings underscore the promise of this approach, further investigation is required to determine whether the observed extent of APOE ε4 knockdown provides sufficient benefits against AD‐related pathologies. Future research should focus on determining the optimal intervention windows for APOE ε4 knockdown, conducting long‐term studies to evaluate the persistence of gene editing and its impact on disease progression to reflect global disease‐based changes, and evaluating cognitive improvements through behavioral studies. We acknowledge that behavioral assessments—such as the Morris water maze (MWM), novel object recognition (NOR), and contextual fear conditioning (CFC)—will be necessary to conclusively evaluate the impact of APOE ε4 knockdown on disease progression and cognitive decline. 76 We plan to address this in future studies. Prior research has shown that reducing astrocytic APOE4 expression in 5.5‐month‐old mice can rescue nest‐building behavior, 53 supporting the expectation that APOE ε4 knockdown may similarly improve cognitive function. Moreover, given that AD primarily affects middle‐aged and older individuals, performing APOE ε4 knockdown in aged and symptomatic mice is critical for evaluating translational relevance. However, the optimal dosing remains uncertain. Although the increased body weight of aged mice may necessitate a higher absolute dose, aging and APOE ε4 expression itself are associated with BBB breakdown, 77 which could result in greater BBBO volumes following identical FUS parameters. 78 This, in turn, may enhance viral delivery efficiency and potentially reduce the required dose. In addition, investigations using more sophisticated transgenic AD mouse models and NHP that better recapitulate human AD pathology will further clarify the full therapeutic potential of APOE ε4 knockdown. 79 Overall, our work serves as a proof‐of‐concept for FUS‐mediated systemic delivery of CRISPR‐based AAVs for gene editing in the brain, providing a promising alternative treatment strategy to reduce apoE4 expression in APOE ε4 carriers for potential LOAD therapy.
